**Distribution of the maximum of 3 cards** (there are C(11,3) = 165 possible hands)

| Max card | Count of cards ≤ this value | P(max ≤ value) | P(max = value) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | 0/165 | 0 |
| 1 | 6 | 20/165 | 20/165 |
| 2 | 7 | 35/165 | 15/165 |
| 6 | 8 | 56/165 | 21/165 |
| 8 | 10 | 120/165 | 64/165 |
| 12 | 11 | 165/165 | 45/165 |

The expected value is (20 + 30 + 126 + 512 + 540) / 165 = 1228 / 165 ≈ 7.44.

**Choosing the quote**
- The settlement value is lumpy: 34% of the time it is 6 or lower, 39% it is 8, and 27% it is 12.
- Averaged over the three possible values, alpha is about 0.48, so roughly half the counterparties may be informed. That calls for a wide spread.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 5, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Before anything is revealed, the expected settlement value is about **6.21**. I'm quoting **5.0 / 7.4** around it.

**Expected value.** I took the expected maximum for each face of die 1 and averaged over its 8 faces:

| Die 1 face | Expected max | Working |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3.00 | Die 2 alone averages 18/6 |
| 2 | 3.50 | max(2, die 2) averages 21/6 |
| 5 | 5.17 | max(5, die 2) averages 31/6 |
| 7 (×3) | 7 each | Die 2 never exceeds 7 |
| 8 | 8 | |
| 9 | 9 | |

The sum is 49.67, and 49.67 / 8 ≈ **6.21**.

**Why the spread is wide.** The share of informed traders is unknown, and its expected value is about 0.48. The outcomes are also bunched at 7 or above:
- **Ask at 7.4:** an informed buyer only takes it when the value is 8 or 9, which has probability 1/4.
- **Bid at 5.0:** an informed seller only hits it when the value is below 5, which has probability about 1/6.
- **Noise traders:** their valuations sit around 6.2 with a standard deviation of 1.5, so some of them will still trade on each side.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.4}

| Die 1 | Probability | Expected max | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1/8 | 3.0 | The max is just die 2, which averages 3. |
| 2 | 1/8 | 3.5 | Die 2's three 1s become 2. |
| 5 | 1/8 | 5.17 | The max is 5 unless die 2 shows 6. |
| 7, 7, 7, 8, 9 | 5/8 | 7.6 | Die 1 is always the max here. |

The weighted total is 49.67 / 8 ≈ 6.21.

**Quote choice:**
- **Ask:** An informed trader buys above 7.4 only when the value is 8 or 9 (probability 1/4). Dropping the ask below 7 would also give away the large mass at 7, so I keep it at 7.4.
- **Bid:** Values below 5 occur with probability about 1/6. A bid around 5.1 keeps that adverse selection small while still catching noise traders, whose valuations centre near 6.2 with standard deviation 1.5.
- **Last quote's no-trade:** It barely moves the fair value, so I keep the quote roughly centred on it.

{"bid": 5.1, "ask": 7.4}

Die 1 came up 7, and die 2's largest face is 6, so the contract will settle at exactly 7. Nothing about the value is uncertain now.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at 7, so they never trade against a bid below 7 or an ask above 7.
- **Noise traders:** their valuations are 7 plus noise with standard deviation 1.5. Any trade with them is profit.
- **Best spread:** expected profit per side is d·P(noise > d). This peaks at d ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 1.1.

So I quote 1.1 either side of 7.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Die 1 came up 7, and every face of die 2 (1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6) is at most 7. So the contract settles at exactly 7 for certain.

- **Noise traders:** their valuations are centred on the public fair value of 7, with standard deviation 1.5.
- **Choosing the spread:** I want the half-spread s that maximises s × P(noise > 7 + s).
  - At s = 1.1 this is about 1.1 × 0.232 ≈ 0.255.
  - At s = 1.2 it is about 1.2 × 0.212 ≈ 0.254.

game.title: Dice/cards product
game.description: A custom deck of 14 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 1, 2 cards worth 2, 1 card worth 7, 3 cards worth 8, 3 cards worth 12, 2 cards worth 15. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The fair value is the expected product of two cards drawn without replacement.

- **Card values:** the sum of all 14 card values is 102, and the sum of their squares is 1132.
- **Expected product:** E[XY] = (102² − 1132) / (14·13) = 9272 / 182 ≈ 51.
- **Risk of informed traders:** settlement ranges from 0 to 225. About 27% of deals contain a 0, so the settlement is often far from 51.
- **Quote:** I don't know the share of informed traders, which could be up to 90%. Noise traders' valuations vary by about 41 around fair value. So I quote a wide spread around 51.

Card 1 is 0, so the product is 0 no matter what card 2 is. The contract will settle at exactly 0, and everyone knows it.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at 0. They will never buy from me at a positive ask. They would only sell to me at a bid above 0, which would be a sure loss for me. So I won't quote a bid.
- **Noise traders** value it at 0 plus Normal(0, 41) noise. I want the ask that maximises ask × P(noise > ask). That works out to about 0.75 × 41 ≈ 31, with an expected gain of about 7 per noise trader.

I am long 2, so selling also brings my position back toward flat, and I have room to sell on both remaining quotes.

- **Bid at −1:** A noise trader sells if its valuation is below −1, and I receive 1 for each unit. An informed trader won't sell at −1. Buying one unit takes my position from +2 to +3, which is still within the limit.

Either trade gains 1, and neither quote can lose money against an informed trader.

**Prior expected value of the product.** The 14 cards sum to S = 102, and their squares sum to Q = 1132. With two cards dealt without replacement:

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description: A custom deck of 19 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 3, 2 cards worth 5, 2 cards worth 7, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 10, 4 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dealt cards showing at least 8.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is about 17.4. I quote **9.9 / 28**. Each side is placed just short of the next informed-trader settlement level.

**Settlement distribution.** 11 of the 19 cards are worth at least 8 (three 9s, four 10s and four 15s). Three cards are dealt.
- The expected count of high cards is 3 × 11/19 ≈ 1.74, so the expected value is about 17.4.
- P(value 0) = 56/969 ≈ 0.058
- P(value 10) = 308/969 ≈ 0.318
- P(value 20) = 440/969 ≈ 0.454
- P(value 30) = 165/969 ≈ 0.170

**Assumption on informed traders.** I use the average alpha, about 0.48, for the share of informed counterparties.

**Bid side.** A bid of 9.9 sits just below 10, so an informed trader sells to me only when the value is 0.
- Expected loss from informed sellers is about 0.57 × alpha.
- Expected gain from noise sellers is about 0.69 × (1 − alpha).
- At alpha ≈ 0.48, the gain (about 0.36) beats the loss (about 0.27).
- Any bid above 10 also takes informed selling when the value is 10, and the result turns negative.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 30.
- Asks in the low 20s pay that trader too much on the value-30 outcome.
- At an ask of 28, the expected informed loss (about 0.16) roughly equals the expected noise gain (about 0.16).
- This keeps exposure small while I learn about alpha from the early trades.

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 28}

No trade on the last quote fits either a noise trader or an informed trader whose value was 10 or 20. That nudges me slightly toward the middle outcomes. Fair value stays around 17.4.

**Settlement distribution.** Eleven of the 19 cards are worth at least 8 (three 9s, four 10s and four 15s). With 3 cards dealt:

| Cards ≥ 8 | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0.058 |
| 1 | 10 | 0.318 |
| 2 | 20 | 0.454 |
| 3 | 30 | 0.170 |

That gives an expected value of 3 × 11/19 × 10 ≈ 17.4.

**Quote.**
- **Ask at 20.1:** an informed trader only buys when the settlement is 30. A value of 20 would not lift the offer.
- **Bid at 12.5:** an informed trader sells only when the settlement is 0 or 10. The bid sits close enough to fair value to still trade with noise traders.

- P(exactly one) = 77/153 ≈ 0.503
- P(both) = 55/153 ≈ 0.359

The fair value is therefore about 12.2. The possible settlement values are 0, 10 and 20.

I don't yet know what share of counterparties are informed, so I'm protecting against them:
- **Ask at 19.9:** an informed trader only buys if the contract settles at 20, and then I lose just 0.1. Noise traders still buy about 8% of the time, at a good margin.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 19.9}

The settlement value is about 12.2. Card 1 was a 3, a low card, so 18 cards remain: 11 are high (at least 8) and 7 are low.

The remaining two cards give these outcomes:

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.137 |
| 10 | 0.503 |

The quote sits wide because informed traders could be common. Bid 9.9, ask 30.

| High cards | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|

  - At an ask of 22, the expected result is about −0.16 per quote.

**Ask:** A tight ask near 20 loses to informed buyers whenever the value is 30, which happens 17% of the time. With alpha this uncertain, every ask I checked comes out near or below break-even. An ask of 24 is about −0.09 per quote and 27 is about −0.03. I'll quote 26, near break-even, mainly to stay in the market and learn something about alpha from whether anyone trades.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.1 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.6 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 7 × E[p]. E[p] = 0.4·0.1 + 0.3·0.2 + 0.3·0.6 = 0.28, so the expected value is about 1.96.

The outcome is very spread out: a p=0.6 coin averages about 4.2 heads, while the low-bias coins average 0.7–1.4. The informed share of traders is unknown and averages about 0.48. So I'll quote a fairly wide spread around 2.0.

At these levels, losses to informed traders roughly offset gains from noise traders, so I expect to break even. Watching how traders hit the quote also tells me something about the informed share.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

The prior expected settlement is about 1.96 heads. The expected chance of heads is 0.4×0.1 + 0.3×0.2 + 0.3×0.6 = 0.28, and 7 × 0.28 = 1.96.

The distribution has two humps. About a quarter of the time there are 0 heads. About a fifth of the time the 0.6 coin was picked and there are 4 or more heads.

The informed share of counterparties averages about 0.48 across the three possible values. That makes informed traders costly on both sides. They sell into any bid when the result is 0, and they buy at the ask when the result is 4 or more.

The last quote (0.6 / 3.4) got no trade, which tells me little. I'll keep the quote wide and push the ask a bit higher than last time, because the high-value tail is the bigger risk.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.6}

Given flip 1 = 0 and flip 2 = 1, I update the coin probabilities, centre the quote on the expected settlement, and set each side just past an integer settlement value.

**Posterior on the coin.** The chance of seeing tails then heads is p(1−p) for each coin. Weighting by the prior gives:
- p = 0.1: 0.4 × 0.09 = 0.036, so posterior ≈ 0.23
- p = 0.2: 0.3 × 0.16 = 0.048, so posterior ≈ 0.31
- p = 0.6: 0.3 × 0.24 = 0.072, so posterior ≈ 0.46

The expected heads probability is about 0.36. Five flips remain, so the expected settlement is 1 + 5 × 0.36 ≈ 2.8.

**Quote placement.** Settlement is always a whole number, so I place each side just inside an integer.
- **Bid 2.0:** an informed trader sells only if settlement is 1. That has about a 24% chance, and I would lose 1.0. A noise trader sells about 27% of the time, and I gain about 0.8.
- **Ask 3.9:** an informed trader buys only if settlement is 4 or more, about a 33% chance. Raising the ask from 3.6 to 3.9 lets in no extra informed trades but earns more on each noise trade. A noise trader buys about 20% of the time, and I gain about 1.1.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 3.9}

Given flips 0 and 1, the fair value is about 2.81.

**Posterior on the coin.** The chance of seeing tails then heads is p(1−p) for each coin. Weighting by the prior gives:

| P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood p(1−p) | Weight | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 0.4 | 0.09 | 0.036 | 0.231 |
| 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.16 | 0.048 | 0.308 |
| 0.6 | 0.3 | 0.24 | 0.072 | 0.462 |

- The expected P(heads) is 0.362.
- With 5 flips left, I expect about 1.81 more heads.
- Adding the 1 head already shown gives a fair value of 2.81.

**Bid side.** The settlement value is a whole number from 1 to 6.
- At a bid of 1.0, an informed seller only trades when the value is 1. That costs me nothing, because I would buy at 1.0 something worth 1.
- Noise traders still sell at that bid about 8% of the time, gaining me about 1.81 each.
- I tested other bids at alpha = 0.5, about its expected value of 0.48. Every bid from 1.0 upward was positive, and the gain grew steadily as the bid fell to 1.0. Going lower than 1.0 just loses noise trades.

**Ask side.** The informed loss comes almost entirely from the 0.6 coin landing 4 or 5 more heads (values 5 or 6). I tested asks at alpha = 0.5:

| Ask | Net expected gain |
|---|---|
| 3.9 | about 0 |
| 4.2 | 0.018 |
| 4.5 | 0.025 |
| 4.8 | 0.029 |
| 5.0 | 0.032 |
| 5.9 | under 0.01 |

The ask works best around 4.8–5.0, and I'll quote 4.9.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.9}

Quote **bid 0.0, ask 7.0**. The settlement distribution is skewed, so only a very low bid pays off.

**Prior value.** Expected heads per flip is 0.4×0.1 + 0.3×0.2 + 0.3×0.6 = 0.28. Over 7 flips the expected settlement is 1.96.

**Settlement distribution.** This is a mixture of three binomials, one per coin. P(V=0) ≈ 0.255 and P(V=1) ≈ 0.264. The right tail is heavy: P(V≥4) ≈ 0.22, driven almost entirely by the 0.6 coin.

**Alpha.** Round 1 had no trades, so it tells us little. The prior mean of alpha is about 0.48.

**Ask side.**
- An ask at 3.5 to 4.5 has negative expected value. Informed buyers in the fat right tail cost more than the noise flow earns.
- For example, at 4.5 the expected value is 0.52×0.066 − 0.48×0.118 < 0.
- An ask at 7 cannot be hit by an informed trader, since the value can never exceed 7. It costs nothing.

**Bid side.**
- At a bid of 0, informed sellers cannot hurt me, because settlement is at least 0.
- Noise traders sell with probability about 0.066 and give about 1.96 of edge each time.
- That is worth about 0.067 per quote, the best of the bids I checked (0.1, 0.3 and 0.5 all scored lower).

{"bid": 0, "ask": 7}

Without any flips revealed, the expected number of heads is 7 × E[p] = 7 × 0.28 ≈ 1.96. The share of informed traders (alpha) is unknown, and my prior average is about 0.48. With that much informed flow, tight quotes look unprofitable.

- That is a net loss unless alpha is low, so I keep the ask wide at 4.5.

**Bid side.**
- A settlement of 0 has probability about 0.25.

- That is roughly break-even to slightly positive, and a fill would also tell me something about alpha.

- If alpha is near its average of about 0.48, the ask side has small positive expected profit.

**Bid side.** A bid of 1.5 is hit by informed traders only when the settlement is 1, which has probability about 0.24.
- I lose 0.5 per informed trade.
- Noise traders sell with probability about 0.16, and I gain about 1.31 per trade.
- This is positive expected profit, and better than a tighter bid of 1.9 or 2.0.

**Fair value is about 1.5. Bid 0.9, ask 3.6.**

**Estimate before the last trade.** Flip 1 was tails and flip 2 was heads. After those two flips, the coin probabilities are about 0.23 for the 0.1 coin, 0.31 for the 0.2 coin and 0.46 for the 0.6 coin.

- Putting this together, P(settlement = 1) ≈ 0.80. If it isn't 1, the expected settlement is about 3.4.

**Bid at 0.9.** The settlement can't be below 1, so an informed trader never sells to me at 0.9. A noise trader sells at that price about a third of the time, and each such trade earns about 0.57.

**Ask at 3.6.** A low ask would mostly be lifted by informed traders who know the settlement is 3 or more, which loses money. A high ask keeps that loss small and still occasionally catches a noise buyer.

{"bid": 0.9, "ask": 3.6}

Before any flips are revealed, each flip is heads with probability 0.4×0.1 + 0.3×0.2 + 0.3×0.6 = 0.28. So the fair value is 7 × 0.28 ≈ 1.96.

game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 3, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 3, 6, 10, 11.
game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the dice.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 0.6 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
I'll quote wide on this first trade.

**Expected value.** The average P(heads) is 0.5·0.2 + 0.4·0.6 + 0.1·0.9 = 0.43. That gives 7 × 0.43 = 3.01 expected heads, so the fair value is about 15.05.

**Spread.** The settlement value has a standard deviation of about 10.3. The share of informed traders could be as high as 0.9, so I set a wide spread.

**Price levels.** Settlement values fall on multiples of 5, so I placed each quote just inside one of those levels.

- **Bid 5.9:** an informed trader sells only if the value is 0 or 5. The expected loss in those cases is small, about 2.6 per trade.
- **Ask 24.1:** an informed trader buys only if the value is 25 or more. The expected loss there is about 3.4 per trade.
- **Noise traders:** each side earns about 9 from noise traders, which roughly offsets the expected informed losses.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 24.1}

The contract's expected value before any information is about 15.05:

- **Expected chance of heads:** 0.5×0.2 + 0.4×0.6 + 0.1×0.9 = 0.43.
- **Expected heads in 7 flips:** 7 × 0.43 ≈ 3.01.
- **Expected settlement:** 3.01 heads × 5 ≈ 15.05.

The last quote of 5.9 / 24.1 drew no trade. An informed trader would have traded whenever the settlement fell outside that range, which means 1 or fewer heads or 5 or more. That happens fairly often, especially with the low-bias coin, where 0 or 1 heads has about a 58% chance. So no trade slightly suggests informed traders are less common and that the value is near the middle. Fair value stays around 15.

I'm tightening the quote a little to invite noise trades. I'm still keeping a wide spread because the share of informed traders is unknown and the possible settlement values are spread out.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 21.5}

Two tails so far shift the belief toward the 0.2 coin. Fair value is about 6.7, so I quote roughly 1 to 12.5.

**Belief about the coin after flips 1 and 2 both came up tails**

| Coin P(heads) | Prior | Chance of two tails | Updated weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.5 | 0.64 | 0.831 |
| 0.6 | 0.4 | 0.16 | 0.166 |
| 0.9 | 0.1 | 0.01 | 0.003 |

- The expected chance of heads is now about 0.268.
- Five flips remain, so I expect about 1.34 more heads.
- That puts fair value at about 6.7.
- The two stage-1 quotes drew no trades, which tells me little.

**Likely settlement values**

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | about 27% |
| 5 | about 35% |
| 10 | about 21% |
| 15 | about 10% |
| 20 or more | about 7% |

**Bid side**
- An informed seller only hits a bid below 5 when the contract will settle at 0.
- So my loss to informed traders is about 0.27 × bid.
- Noise sellers still hit a low bid fairly often, because their noise has a standard deviation of 7.2.
- Lowering the bid steadily improves expected profit at a middling alpha:

| Bid | Expected profit at alpha 0.5 |
|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.33 |
| 1.5 | 0.41 |
| 1.0 | 0.47 |
| 0.5 | 0.53 |

- I choose about 1.0.

**Ask side**
- With an ask between 10 and 15, informed buyers come only when settlement is 15 or more (about 17%).
- Their average value in that case is about 17.4.
- An ask of about 12.5 balances the loss to informed buyers against the gain from noise buyers, so I choose 12.5.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 12.5}

Quote: bid 0, ask 14.9. This is the last quote of the round, so I only need the best expected profit on this one trade.

**Fair value.** Starting chances for the coin: P(heads) = 0.2 at 50%, 0.6 at 40%, 0.9 at 10%. After two tails these update to about 83%, 17% and 0.3%.
- The expected P(heads) is now about 0.288.
- The 5 remaining flips should give about 1.44 more heads.
- So the fair value is about 7.2.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement can only be 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25, with probabilities of about 27%, 35%, 21%, 10%, 5% and 1%.

**Bid.** I bid 0, which costs nothing.
- An informed trader only sells if the value is below the bid, and the value can never be below 0.
- Noise traders still sell when their valuation falls below 0, which happens about 16% of the time.
- That gives an expected gain of about 1.1 per noise counterparty.
- Any bid between 0 and 5 is hit by informed traders whenever settlement is 0 (27% chance), which costs more than it gains.

**Ask.** I set the ask just below 15 to keep noise-trader flow while limiting losses to informed buyers. I assume an informed share of about 0.48, roughly the average of the three possible values.
- At 14.9, informed traders buy only when settlement is 15 or more, losing about 0.39 per informed counterparty.
- Noise traders buy about 14% of the time, gaining about 1.1 per noise counterparty.
- The net is about +0.39, which beats asks of 9.9 (negative), 12 (+0.22) and 16 (+0.36).

- **Bid 5.0:** informed traders sell to me only when the value is 0, which has probability about 0.24.
- **Ask 20.0:** informed traders buy from me only when the value is 25 or more, which has probability about 0.19.
- On both sides, the expected loss to informed traders roughly balances the expected gain from noise traders crossing at these levels.

game.description: An urn holds 6 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 6. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.

|---|---|

| 59 | about 0.22 |

A noise trader sells at 0 when its noise is below −10, which happens about 24% of the time, and I gain about 10 on average when that happens. Raising the bid to 1 lets informed sellers in whenever the value is 0 (probability 3/7), so it is worse.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The fair value before any flips is 27.2, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it (bid 20.0, ask 34.4) to protect against informed traders.

- **Expected heads rate:** 0.2·0.2 + 0.4·0.7 + 0.4·0.9 = 0.68.
- **Expected settlement:** 8 flips × 0.68 × 5 = 27.2.

game.description: An urn holds 7 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 7. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 9 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 9. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Quoting wide at bid 10, ask 80, because about half of all counterparties are expected to be informed and a narrower spread loses money.

- **Fair value:** the number of red balls is equally likely to be 0 through 9. So the settlement is equally likely to be any of 0, 10, …, 90, with mean 45.
- **Informed share:** the prior average of alpha is (0.05 + 0.5 + 0.9) / 3 ≈ 0.48.
- **Expected profit by ask level** (the bid side mirrors this):
  - Ask 70: informed traders cost about 3 and noise traders earn about 2.6. Net is roughly −0.1.
  - Ask 75: informed traders cost about 2 and noise traders earn about 2. Net is roughly +0.07.
  - Ask 80: informed traders cost about 1 (only when the value is 90) and noise traders earn about 1.4. Net is roughly +0.24.
- **Choice:** ask 80 is about as good as wider quotes and still trades often enough to show me what kind of counterparties I face. The mirror on the other side of 45 is bid 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 80}

The prior fair value is still 45. The settlement value is equally likely to be any of 0, 10, …, 90, so the mean is 45 and the standard deviation is about 28.7. The 10/80 quote that drew no trade is symmetric, so it does not move the fair value. It slightly favours a low alpha, but only slightly.

Taking alpha at its average of about 0.48, I compared ask levels using 0.52 × (gain from noise traders) minus 0.48 × (loss to informed traders). Bids follow by symmetry.

| Ask | Loss per informed arrival | Gain per noise arrival | Weighted net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 70 | 3.0 | 2.64 | −0.07 |
| 75 | 2.0 | 2.0 | +0.08 |
| 78 | 1.4 | 1.63 | +0.18 |
| 80 | 1.0 | 1.40 | +0.25 |

A spread of about ±35 around 45 is the best of these, so I am keeping the same quote.

The two no-trade quotes at 10/80 in stage 1 make R = 9 less likely, since an informed trader would have bought at 80 then. That pulls fair value down to about 59–60, with a standard deviation of roughly 21.

Alpha could be as high as 0.9, so I'm keeping the spread wide.
- **Ask at 80:** the expected loss to informed buyers is small (only R = 9, worth 90, is above it). Noise traders still buy about 15% of the time at roughly 20 above fair.
- **Bid at 30:** an informed seller only trades when R ≤ 2, which is unlikely given a red draw. Noise traders sell about 7% of the time at roughly 30 below fair.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 80}

Given that draw 1 was red, the posterior on the number of red balls R is proportional to R. That gives E[R] = 285/45 ≈ 6.33, so the public fair value is about 63.3. The settlement value is 10R, with P(R = r) = r/45.

I average over the three possible values of alpha, which gives an expected alpha of about 0.48. For each candidate price I weigh the expected loss to informed traders against the expected gain from noise traders, whose valuations are 63.3 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 20.

**Ask side**
- At an ask of 90, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 90.
- A noise trader still buys about 9% of the time and pays about 27 above fair value.
- This is the best ask of those I checked (75, 85, 89, 90, 91), at about +1.26 expected.

**Bid side**
- Expected profit is roughly flat at about +0.4 for bids between 30 and 40.
- At 35, an informed trader sells only when R is 3 or fewer, costing about 0.75 in expectation.
- That is more than covered by noise traders, who sell about 8% of the time at roughly 28 below fair value.

{"bid": 35, "ask": 90}

Quoting 5 / 85. A tight market loses money here because informed traders pick it off, and the chance of meeting one is likely high.

**Value before any reveal.** The number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 9, so the contract value is uniform on {0, 10, …, 90}. Its mean is 45 and its standard deviation is about 29.

**Who trades.**
- Noise traders value the contract at 45 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 20. They give me profit equal to my distance from 45, times the chance they cross my quote.
- Informed traders only trade when they beat my quote. On the ask side, I lose (true value − ask) whenever the true value is above my ask.
- The chance of an informed trader is unknown, but its prior average is about 0.48. Round 1 had no trades, which tells me almost nothing about it.

| Ask | Expected profit |

| 65 | about −0.5 |
| 75 | about +0.07 |

| 85 | about +0.23 |
| 90 | about +0.28 |

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. Each ball was independently painted red with probability 0.6. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
No trades yet, so my quote is set by the prior and by adverse selection.

**Prior on the settlement value.** The number of red balls V is Binomial(10, 0.6). Its mean is 6 and its standard deviation is about 1.55.

**Adverse selection.** Alpha is unknown, and its prior mean is about 0.48. That means roughly half of the counterparties could know V exactly.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer trades only when V is above my ask. A noise trader buys when 6 plus Normal(0, 1.1) noise is above my ask.
- At 7.0 or 7.1, expected gains from noise traders roughly equal or fall short of expected losses to informed buyers.
- At 7.9, an informed buyer only trades when V is 8 or more. My expected loss to them is about 0.07, weighted by alpha. My expected gain from noise traders is about 0.08, weighted by 1 − alpha. That gives a small positive edge.

**Bid side.** The same calculation, mirrored, gives a slightly positive edge at a bid of 4.0.

So I quote wide: bid 4.0, ask 7.9. Early trades will also help me learn alpha.

game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.
